issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: 'Lost Community and culture' is not impossible for a combat trauma survivor, but for a 49-year-old married male European city council member it is the least coherent appraisal in this profile and is weakly anchored to the rest of the selected nodes. The rest of the profile centers on bodily danger, touch/startle, fragmented trauma recall, and safety distrust; this item instead implies a culturally/community dislocation theme that is not supported elsewhere in Triggers/Threat/Memory/Maladaptive Strategies.

issues.item: Memory: Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
issues.explanation: 'Overwhelming grief on recall' is not inherently inconsistent, but here it is the least coherent memory item relative to the formulation and other selected items. The profile is dominated by fear-based threat, bodily vulnerability, touch alarm, and cognitive disorganization of recall. A grief-dominant recall item without corresponding loss/bereavement appraisals or related strategies makes the memory cluster less internally aligned.

issues.item: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: The profile is largely coherent for a middle-aged male combat survivor, but this appraisal is the main mismatch. 'My body has been permanently damaged' implies a salient lasting physical injury. That idea is not supported elsewhere in the selected profile: memory items focus on fragmented, terror-laden recall; threat items emphasize current danger, mistrust of safety, startle to touch, and sleep disturbance; maladaptive strategies emphasize sensory distraction, thought monitoring, and avoidance of touch. There are no triggers selected, and no other items indicate ongoing medical consequences or trauma themes centered on bodily injury. In this profile, the appraisal reads as if it belongs to a different subtype centered on physical injury rather than the represented combat-related fear/terror formulation.

issues.item: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For a combat trauma profile in a 49-year-old male, this specific self-blame item is the main coherence problem. The rest of the profile centers on persistent danger, touch-triggered alarm, fragmented/terror-laden memory, and defensive avoidance, which fits combat-related PTSD. In contrast, 'the event happened because of the way I acted' implies a strong internal-causal guilt formulation that is not otherwise supported by the selected memory, threat, or strategy items. This makes the appraisal set less coherent with the overall profile and with the formulation, where Memory and Threat strongly feed Negative Appraisals focused on ongoing danger rather than responsibility for causing the trauma. Self-blame can occur in combat PTSD, but here it is insufficiently connected to the other selected items and stands out as the least clinically coherent item.

vignette:
Daniel Mercer, a 49-year-old European American city council member, first noticed that the war had not ended for him in the years after his deployment when ordinary life began to feel arranged around danger. During a convoy mission in Afghanistan, an explosion tore through the vehicle ahead of his, leaving him pinned under shouting, dust, and the metallic smell of blood while he tried to make sense of broken radio calls and flashes of bodies moving in and out of view. What stayed with Daniel was not a clean story but fragments: the blast itself, a gloved hand, someone screaming his name, and then gaps he could not fill. Even now, when he tries to explain what happened, he loses the thread halfway through and is left embarrassed and angry with himself. Remembering it brings back the same terror he felt in the moment, and the missing pieces make him feel as if the danger is still unfinished, still waiting to be identified.

In the years that followed, Daniel came to believe that his own body had betrayed him. He described it as reacting before he could think, jerking hard when a spouse brushed past him unexpectedly in the kitchen or when staff in the council office came up behind his chair. He had become convinced that the world was a dangerous place and that he had to be on guard all the time, because even when others assured him he was safe he could not believe it. That conviction sharpened every jolt of alarm: a sudden touch, a slammed door in City Hall, footsteps in a hallway after a late meeting. Those moments sent him back to the same half-remembered terror, and the alarm made the gaps in his memory feel more ominous, as though the missing details must contain something he had failed to notice.

To keep himself from being swallowed by that uncertainty, Daniel developed a set of habits that shaped his days. He put on loud music or left the television on for hours, filling the house with noise so there was less room to notice the images that came up when things were quiet. He monitored his thoughts constantly for signs that he was "going crazy," checking himself for drift, for images, for any hint that he might be losing control. He also avoided being touched in almost any form, pulling away from his wife when she reached for his arm and stiffening when constituents tried to shake his hand at public events. At first these strategies gave him a brief sense of control, but they also made the memory more slippery. When he drowned out silence and kept scanning his mind, the fragments of the blast never settled into a coherent account, and the story remained broken in the same places. The less he could tell clearly, the more certain he became that something was badly wrong with him, that his body's reactions and his fragmented recall meant he was still unsafe, still damaged.

That conviction fed the vigilance. Daniel started watching doorways, parking lots, and the expressions of people around him with the seriousness of someone on patrol, and he slept badly, lying awake after council meetings or waking at 3 a.m. with his heart racing and the television still murmuring in the next room. The poor sleep left him more on edge the next day, and the added strain made every unexpected touch or sudden noise feel sharper. In turn, those alarms brought the battlefield back into his mind in flashes, and with each return he felt again that same hot surge of fear, followed by the thought that his body was still stuck in the war. He found himself retreating further into noise, into thought-checking, into distance from others, and each retreat made it harder for him to gather the memory into words or to trust that the present day was different from the one he survived overseas.

By the time he sought help, the cost had become hard to ignore. At home, his wife had stopped trying to comfort him by touch because he flinched so often; at work, he had begun avoiding crowded receptions and staying close to exits at public meetings, which colleagues noticed but did not understand. Daniel was not asking for reassurance so much as for relief from the exhausting certainty that he was permanently on guard. What frightened him most was the fear that this pattern was becoming his new normal, and what he hoped for, though he struggled to say it plainly, was to sleep without scanning, to remember the event without being pulled back into its terror, and to believe that safety could feel real in his body again.
